fatal_errors: A post-solidification anneal cannot improve glass-forming ability, because it is applied only after the glass has already formed; it could only affect the stability of an existing amorphous state.
The proposed annealing window is defined relative to Tg, but no glass transition was detected for the target alloy, so Tg −5 to Tg −20 °C is not an operationally definable condition.
The hypothesis omits the actual composition-and-cooling intervention: adjusting Fe/Co/Mn, reducing P from 20 to 15 at.%, and rapid melt spinning at 40 m/s.
No prior evidence is supplied despite the request for supporting evidence.
explanation: The response addresses phosphorus-containing multicomponent metallic glasses and offers a testable thermal-stability experiment, but it does not reconstruct the target intervention or mechanism. The target attributes improved glass formation to composition changes that favor eutectic solidification and to rapid quenching that suppresses segregation and phosphide nucleation. In contrast, the proposed sub-Tg anneal is performed after vitrification and therefore cannot improve glass-forming ability as claimed. Its conditions are also incompatible with the target because Tg was not observed. Structural relaxation can change crystallization behavior, but it does not necessarily hinder nucleation and may instead facilitate ordering or nanocrystallization, so that mechanism requires evidence that is absent here. DSC and XRD comparisons could falsify the thermal-stability portion, but the design does not test glass-forming ability; TEM is also not a direct quantitative measure of free volume without a specified method.
